extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, journalists, and media historians researching early-20th-century wire-service/newsroom practices
extracted.subtask_description: Affidavits and testimony describing accepted practices, duties, and procedural rules in wire-service newsrooms (Associated Press and International News Service) circa 1913–1917, including obligations to share news, access to proofs, tipping, prioritization, and restrictions on publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP member duty to furnish all news items
rubrics_metrics.description: "under the bylaws of the Associated Press ... said B. E. Gushing was in duty bound to furnish the Associated Press with all news items, whatever their source."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a bylaw obligation of a newspaper/telegraph editor who was an AP correspondent — implies a co-operative expectation that member papers/representatives must turn over news items to the AP regardless of source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial origination rule for wire bulletins
rubrics_metrics.description: "it was not my business to put anything on the wire, as news, which did not originate in my own district."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported reprimand from New York (signed "B F"). Imposes a practical limit that bureau managers should not transmit as news items material that did not originate in their assigned district without authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sending rewrites or unauthorized bulletins
rubrics_metrics.description: "I received a message and instruction from the New York office ... that I must, under no circumstances, send out such a bulletin or rewrite news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct instruction from central office forbidding local managers from issuing bulletins that are rewrites of other publications or otherwise not authorized; two cited instances (Peterboro explosion and Birmingham mine cave-in) show the rule being enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent verification when acted on by a tip
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gushing never read me the A.P. story or bulletin, so far as I know; all he ever gave me was a tip as to the nature, character and source of the story. It was up to us to get our information, then, as best we could."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice described where tips (about AP items) were given but the bureau was expected to obtain its own information through its resources rather than simply re-transmitting the competitor's copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization requests to central office to expedite stories
rubrics_metrics.description: "it has been my custom whenever I could do it, to accommodate our clients when advised of their wishes, to message New York to put on the wire the particular story in which they are interested, first, so that they might have the advantage of publishing it as early as they wished to."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers would request New York to prioritize sending a particular story ahead of other material to serve local clients' edition deadlines (example: urgings to speed the Powhatan fire story). This is an operational practice used to secure early publication for subscribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated Press access to pre-publication proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: "the Associated Press ... had access to the proofs of copy edited and headed for publication in the Cleveland News; that said privilege enabled the Associated Press to see such proofs before the news contained in such proofs had been published in the Cleveland News."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP had physical/practical access to proofs (local and telegraph/cable copy) prior to publication — a procedural privilege that could affect timeliness and confidentiality of local reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation from wire services to newspaper staff (conflict-of-interest risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple statements: e.g., "said B. E. Gushing ... received for the [Associated Press] service a compensation of Ten Dollars ($10.00) per week" and that smaller sums (Three Dollars) were paid to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits document payments from a wire service to a newspaper telegraph editor and onward payments to assistants; indicates an economic relationship that may create conflicts of interest between newsroom duties and wire-service obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rapid internal channels (telephone, pneumatic tube) to tip wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of methods used: calling AP by telephone with prompts such as "Hearst says forty dead ... What have you?" and sending stories/proofs via pneumatic tube to AP offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephone and pneumatic-tube systems were explicitly used for immediate tips and for transmitting rewrites/proofs to a wire service — operational channels enabling rapid (sometimes secret) transfer of information between a paper and a wire service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on AP employees' access to composing-room proofs (with practical exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: "there was a rule put into effect which prevented Associated Press employes from going into the composing room for proofs of news, but this rule, of course, did not apply to Gushing in his capacity as Telegraph Editor of the said Cleveland News."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal rule limiting AP staff access to proof material existed, but enforcement had exceptions when a newspaper staffer also served as an AP correspondent/editor, illustrating a tension between formal policy and operational practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt notification to local papers for extras/special editions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would at once message to New York, with the idea of getting an International News Service story for the Cleveland News, and for my Ohio State wire, so that I could legitimately serve our own subscribers with the same story ... and I immediately called up Cushing of the Cleveland News to tell him its contents so that the Cleveland News could issue an extra or special edition if they chose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice of immediately informing a client paper (or calling a local editor) about bulletins/flash news so they could decide to publish an extra edition; demonstrates operational coordination aimed at timeliness for print deadlines.
